title: The Death of the Funnel: Why Flywheels Win
excerpt: Traditional funnels fail to capture the compounding value of customer retention. Here is how to engineer a revenue flywheel.
content:
The sales funnel was designed in 1898. It was built for a world where customers had limited information, sales reps had the leverage, and retention was someone else's problem. That world no longer exists.

Yet most revenue organisations still run on funnel logic. They measure top-of-funnel volume, optimise conversion at each stage, and celebrate closed-won. What happens after the contract is signed is left to Customer Success — a team that is structurally disconnected from the rest of the revenue system.

This is not a process problem. It is an architectural one.

What the Funnel Actually Measures

The funnel is a one-directional model. Energy enters at the top, gets processed through the stages, and exits as a closed deal. Every stage leaks. The goal is to minimise loss.

What this model cannot capture is compounding value. A customer who renews, expands, and refers is worth an order of magnitude more than their initial contract. But in a funnel model, they simply fall out of the bottom and reappear at the top of another funnel if you want to sell them more.

The metrics that emerge from funnel thinking reflect this limitation. New ARR, pipeline coverage, close rate — all of these measure the efficiency of acquisition. None of them measure the health of the revenue you already have.

How a Flywheel Works Differently

A flywheel does not have a top or a bottom. It has momentum. The more energy you put into it, the faster it spins — and critically, a well-designed flywheel generates its own energy over time.

In a revenue flywheel, acquisition feeds retention, retention feeds expansion, and expansion feeds acquisition through referrals, case studies, and reputation. Each rotation compounds the last.

The key structural difference is that customers are not outputs of the system — they are part of the engine. Your best customers reduce your cost of acquisition. They validate your positioning. They shrink your sales cycle for similar profiles. A funnel discards this value entirely.

The Three Engines

A working revenue flywheel has three engines that must be aligned and instrumented.

Acquisition is still important — but its job changes. Instead of filling the top of a funnel with volume, it should be precision-targeting the profiles most likely to retain and expand. ICP sharpness matters more than lead volume. Marketing and Sales need a shared definition of what a good customer actually looks like, built from retention data, not assumptions.

Retention is the flywheel's core. If customers do not stay, nothing compounds. This means onboarding must be engineered, not improvised. Time-to-value must be measured. CS must have visibility into product usage, engagement signals, and health scores — not just renewal dates. Churn is not a CS problem; it is a system failure that begins long before the renewal conversation.

Expansion is the highest-margin revenue you will ever generate. No new acquisition cost, no lengthy sales cycle — just a customer who already trusts you, buying more. This requires a clear expansion motion: defined triggers, ownership, and an offer that maps to the customer's evolving needs. Most companies have expansion revenue that is effectively accidental. Engineering it is one of the highest-leverage activities in RevOps.

What This Means for Your Metrics

Switching to flywheel thinking requires switching your measurement model. Net Revenue Retention becomes the primary health metric — it captures acquisition, retention, and expansion in a single number. An NRR above 100% means your existing customer base is growing without any new logos.

Expansion ARR should be tracked separately from new ARR. Time-to-value and onboarding completion rates become leading indicators of retention risk. Referral rate tells you whether your customers are part of your acquisition engine or not.

These metrics exist in most CRMs. The problem is that they are rarely connected. Acquisition data sits in marketing tools, retention data sits in CS platforms, expansion data sits in a spreadsheet. The flywheel only works when the data is unified.

Engineering the Transition

Moving from funnel to flywheel is not a rebrand. It requires structural changes to how your teams are organised, how your systems are connected, and what you measure.

Start with the data layer. Map where your customer journey data lives and identify the gaps. You cannot optimise what you cannot see. Then define the handover points — the moments where ownership transfers between Marketing, Sales, and CS — and instrument them. Most revenue leakage happens at handovers.

Then align the incentives. If Sales is compensated purely on new ARR and CS is compensated on NPS, the flywheel will never spin. The compensation model must reflect the compounding nature of the system you are trying to build.

The funnel is not wrong. It is incomplete. The companies that outperform their markets in the next five years will not be the ones with the highest lead volume. They will be the ones with the most efficient revenue engine — and that engine is a flywheel.

title: HubSpot vs Salesforce: The 2026 Verdict
excerpt: Choosing your CRM is the most expensive decision you will make this year. We break down the pros and cons for scaling SaaS.
content:
Every year, someone publishes a comparison that concludes with: it depends on your needs. That is true, but not useful. Here is a more direct take — based on what we see inside scaling SaaS businesses every day.

The HubSpot vs Salesforce question is not really about features. Both platforms can, with enough configuration, do most of what the other does. The real question is: what does your organisation actually need right now, what will it need in eighteen months, and what is the true cost of each path?

What Has Changed in 2026

Both platforms have moved aggressively on AI. HubSpot's Breeze AI is embedded natively across the CRM, marketing, and CS hubs — it summarises contacts, drafts sequences, scores leads, and flags churn risk without requiring a separate integration. Salesforce's Einstein has matured significantly, particularly in forecasting and pipeline inspection, but the value is concentrated in Enterprise tiers that carry a corresponding price tag.

HubSpot has also closed the gap on customisation. The introduction of custom objects, calculated properties, and more granular workflow logic means the old criticism — that HubSpot is too rigid for complex revenue models — is less valid than it was. It is not gone entirely, but it is weaker.

Salesforce, meanwhile, has become more expensive to run. Agentforce, its AI agent layer, is powerful in enterprise environments but adds meaningful cost and admin complexity. The platform rewards investment. If you are not prepared to invest, you will not see the returns.

Where HubSpot Wins

For SaaS businesses between £1M and £30M ARR, HubSpot is typically the stronger choice. The reasons are structural, not cosmetic.

Implementation speed. A well-scoped HubSpot implementation can be production-ready in four to eight weeks. Salesforce rarely is. Time matters when your team is selling and you need the system to support them now, not in six months.

Total cost of ownership. HubSpot's licensing is transparent. Salesforce's is not. By the time you add Sales Cloud, Service Cloud, Marketing Cloud, platform fees, and the Salesforce admin you will need to maintain it, the cost is substantially higher than the headline figure suggests.

Native connectivity. Marketing, Sales, and CS in a single platform means your data is unified by default. You do not need a complex integration layer to get a complete view of your customer. For companies building a flywheel revenue model, this is a significant structural advantage.

Adoption. HubSpot is built to be used by salespeople, not administrators. The interface is cleaner, the mobile app is functional, and the learning curve is shorter. CRM value is directly correlated with adoption. A system your team does not use is not a system — it is a liability.

Where Salesforce Wins

Salesforce remains the dominant platform at enterprise scale, and for good reason.

Configurability. If your revenue model is genuinely complex — multi-product, channel-heavy, territory-based, or highly regulated — Salesforce can be shaped to fit it. HubSpot imposes structural assumptions that do not always hold at enterprise level.

Ecosystem depth. The Salesforce AppExchange is the most mature third-party ecosystem in B2B software. If you need deep integrations with ERP systems, complex CPQ processes, or industry-specific tooling, Salesforce is where those integrations exist and are well-maintained.

Forecasting and pipeline intelligence. For large sales organisations managing complex pipeline across multiple product lines and geographies, Salesforce's forecasting engine — particularly with Einstein — is more sophisticated than anything HubSpot currently offers.

Scalability without migration. Companies that have grown into Salesforce rarely leave it. The platform scales to virtually any organisational complexity. If your ambition is to build a company with hundreds of sales reps across multiple geographies, building on Salesforce early avoids a painful migration later.

The Decision Framework

Strip away the marketing and ask three questions.

How complex is your revenue model today? If you have a single product, a relatively straightforward sales motion, and a team under fifty people, HubSpot will serve you better. If you have multi-product lines, channel partners, or complex deal structures, Salesforce earns its complexity.

What is your RevOps maturity? Salesforce rewards dedicated RevOps investment. If you do not have someone who can own the platform — configure it, maintain it, and evolve it — you will pay for a Ferrari and drive it in second gear. HubSpot can be managed by a generalist. Salesforce typically cannot.

What does your data model actually require? Map your customer journey before you choose your CRM. If your journey does not fit into standard objects and stages, understand how each platform handles that before you commit.

The Hidden Cost Nobody Mentions

The most expensive part of a CRM decision is not the licence. It is the organisational cost of a bad implementation — the bad data, the workarounds, the reports nobody trusts, the processes that live in spreadsheets because the CRM could not handle them.

Both platforms can produce this outcome. The differentiator is not which platform you choose — it is whether you design the system before you build it. A well-architected HubSpot implementation will outperform a poorly architected Salesforce implementation every time. The inverse is also true.

Choose the platform that fits your current complexity and your near-term trajectory. Then invest in implementing it properly. The platform debate is secondary to the implementation quality. That is where the real ROI lives.

title: Lifecycle Logic: The Framework Your Customer Journey Is Missing
excerpt: Most customer journey maps are just funnels redrawn. True lifecycle logic starts from the customer's perspective — and it changes everything about how you run revenue.
content:
Ask most revenue teams to show you their customer journey and they will show you a funnel with extra labels. Awareness becomes Prospect. Interest becomes MQL. Decision becomes Opportunity. The stages change; the logic does not.

A genuine lifecycle framework is built from a fundamentally different starting point. It asks: what is the customer experiencing at each stage, and what do they need from us to move forward? Not what does our team need to do to progress the deal — what does the customer need to succeed.

That shift in perspective sounds philosophical. The operational consequences are anything but.

Stages vs Statuses

Before designing a lifecycle framework, it is worth being precise about what a stage actually is.

A lifecycle stage is a distinct phase in the customer relationship that requires a different engagement model, different ownership, and different success metrics. It is not a CRM field that changes when a rep updates a picklist. A status is a snapshot. A stage is a structural state.

Most CRM implementations conflate the two. Teams end up with twenty-three pipeline stages that no one agrees on, lifecycle fields that contradict deal stages, and reports that measure activity rather than progress. The root cause is almost always the same: the stages were designed around internal workflow, not customer reality.

A proper lifecycle framework has six to eight stages maximum. Each one has a clear entry criterion, a clear exit criterion, and a defined owner. If you cannot articulate all three for a given stage, it is not a stage — it is a wish.

Designing Around the Customer, Not the Org Chart

The most common failure in lifecycle design is building the framework around internal team structure. Marketing owns leads. Sales owns opportunities. CS owns accounts. The stages map to the handovers between those teams.

This produces a lifecycle that is legible internally but invisible to the customer. From the customer's perspective, they have a relationship with one company. The fact that three different teams are managing different parts of that relationship — often without full visibility into each other's activity — is your problem, not theirs. But they feel the consequences: repeated questions, misaligned messaging, gaps in service at the handover points.

A customer-centric lifecycle is designed by mapping the customer's experience first. What are they trying to achieve when they first engage with you? What does success look like at thirty days, ninety days, one year? What questions do they have at each stage, and who in your organisation is best placed to answer them?

Once the customer journey is mapped from their perspective, the internal ownership model follows. Not the other way around.

Entry and Exit Criteria: The Most Important Detail Nobody Gets Right

A lifecycle framework without clear criteria is a taxonomy, not a system. The power of lifecycle logic comes from its predictability — if a customer meets criterion X, they move to stage Y, and that triggers action Z. Without defined criteria, the stages are just labels and the system depends on human judgement at every point.

Entry criteria should be objective and verifiable. Not

— that is a judgement, not a criterion. Instead: the prospect has confirmed budget, identified decision-maker, and agreed to a discovery call. Criteria should be observable from system data wherever possible, which means they need to be captured in your CRM, not locked in someone's memory.

Exit criteria are equally important and more commonly skipped. What has to be true for a customer to move from onboarding to active? From active to at-risk? Most teams define forward progression but not regression. This means customers can stay in the wrong stage indefinitely, and the early warning signals for churn get missed.

Lifecycle Stage as the Governing Logic

Once lifecycle stages are properly defined, they become the governing logic for everything downstream. Automation triggers fire based on stage transitions. Reporting is structured around stage distribution and velocity. Compensation models can be tied to stage outcomes rather than activity metrics.

More importantly, lifecycle stage determines communication. A customer in onboarding should receive different messages, different content, and different contact frequency than a customer who has been active for two years. Treating them the same — as most marketing automation does by default — is not just inefficient; it is actively damaging to the relationship.

The practical implication is that your segmentation model must be built on lifecycle stage, not just firmographic data. Industry and company size tell you who the customer is. Lifecycle stage tells you what they need right now. Both are required for communication that feels relevant rather than generic.

Instrumentation: What to Measure at Each Stage

A lifecycle framework is only as good as the data flowing through it. Each stage needs a primary metric that indicates whether the customer is progressing as expected.

In onboarding, the primary metric is time-to-first-value — the point at which the customer has experienced the outcome they bought the product to achieve. Research consistently shows that customers who reach first value within the expected window retain at dramatically higher rates. If your onboarding is unmeasured, you are flying blind on your most important retention lever.

In the active stage, engagement depth and product adoption breadth are the key signals. A customer using one feature of a five-feature product is not the same risk profile as a customer embedded across the platform. Health scores built from usage data give CS teams the ability to intervene before a customer decides to leave — not after.

At the expansion stage, the metrics shift to identifying the trigger conditions that correlate with upsell readiness. These differ by product and market but typically include usage thresholds, team growth signals, or milestone events within the customer's business. Identifying these triggers and building them into your lifecycle system turns expansion from a reactive conversation into a proactive motion.

Building It in Practice

The lifecycle framework does not need to be perfect before it is useful. The goal of the first version is to create shared language and surface the most important gaps in your current system.

Start by mapping your current stages and asking, honestly, whether each one meets the criteria above. Most organisations find that they have more stages than necessary and fewer criteria than they thought. The simplification exercise alone typically improves CRM data quality and reporting accuracy within weeks.

Then identify the two or three stage transitions that matter most to your revenue outcomes. Where is the most value being lost? Where are the handovers most fragmented? Build the entry and exit criteria for those transitions first. Get them into your CRM. Measure the impact. Then expand the framework from there.

Lifecycle logic is not a project. It is an operating model. The companies that get it right do not treat it as a one-time implementation — they treat it as a living system that evolves as their customer base and product grow. That is the difference between a framework that gets filed away and one that actually runs the business.

title: Change Doesn't Scale: Managing RevOps Transformation at Every Stage of Growth
excerpt: Change management fails differently at startups, scale-ups, and enterprises. The tactics that work at 20 people actively damage trust at 200. Here is how to read the room.
content:
Most change management advice is written as if organisations exist on a single point on the growth curve. In practice, a company with fifteen people and a company with fifteen hundred face entirely different change problems — and the tactics that work at one stage often make things worse at the other.

When RevOps transformations fail, the technical design is rarely the root cause. The root cause is almost always a mismatch between the change approach and the organisational reality. The right framework for change at a Series A startup will create resistance, not adoption, at a mature enterprise. The top-down mandate that drives fast alignment in a large company creates resentment in a team of thirty where everyone knows everyone.

Understanding which change mode fits your organisation is not a soft skill. It is a prerequisite for any operational transformation landing successfully.

The Startup Stage: Chaos Tolerance and the Absence of Process

In early-stage companies — typically under fifty people — the dominant dynamic is speed over structure. Decisions are made quickly, roles overlap, and processes are either unwritten or non-existent. This is often by design. Early companies optimise for learning and iteration, not consistency.

The change management challenge at this stage is not resistance to new processes — it is the absence of any process to replace. You are not changing how people work; you are introducing the concept of working in a defined way at all. That is a different problem.

The failure mode here is over-engineering. RevOps consultants and operators who come from larger organisations sometimes arrive at an early-stage company and build infrastructure for a business three times its current size. The team cannot absorb it. They follow the process for two weeks and then revert to doing things the way they always have, because the new system adds friction without visible payoff at their scale.

What works at this stage is ruthless prioritisation. Identify the one or two operational problems that are directly costing revenue — leads falling through the cracks, deals stuck without a next step, no visibility on pipeline — and fix those specifically. Build for the next six months, not the next three years. Earn adoption by delivering visible value quickly. Complexity can come later; credibility must come first.

The other critical factor at this stage is founder buy-in. In small organisations, the founder or CEO sets the behavioural norm. If they use the CRM, the team uses the CRM. If they do not, no amount of training will change that. Change management at startup scale is, in large part, change management for the person at the top.

The Scale-Up Stage: Tribal Knowledge and the Weight of History

Between fifty and two hundred and fifty people, organisations enter the most operationally complex phase of their growth. They are large enough that informal coordination breaks down but not yet large enough to have the management infrastructure of a mature company. Processes exist but are inconsistently applied. Tribal knowledge — the unwritten rules about how things actually work — is everywhere.

The change management challenge here is the hardest of the three stages. You are asking people who built something from nothing to accept that the way they built it needs to change. The resistance is not irrational. These people made the company work. Their instinct to protect what works is reasonable. The job of the change leader is to channel that instinct rather than fight it.

The failure mode at this stage is the top-down mandate without context. Leadership announces a new process, a new tool, or a new structure. The rationale is not explained in terms the team can connect to their daily reality. Adoption is treated as compliance rather than genuine behaviour change. The process is followed in the CRM and ignored in practice.

What works at this stage is involving the people who carry the tribal knowledge in the design process. Not as a consultative gesture, but as genuine co-designers. The people doing the work know where the real friction is. They know which parts of the current system are actually functioning and which parts exist on paper only. Designs built with that knowledge embedded in them are adopted because they solve real problems, not theoretical ones.

Communication must be over-indexed at this stage. Every operational change needs a clear narrative: here is what is changing, here is why, here is what it means for you specifically, and here is what success looks like. The narrative must be repeated across multiple channels and reinforced by managers, not just delivered once in an all-hands and considered done.

The Enterprise Stage: Bureaucracy, Politics, and Integration Complexity

In large organisations — above five hundred people — the primary change management challenge is not adoption. It is alignment. Getting fifty people to agree on a definition, a process, or a data standard is harder than building the process itself. And the consequences of getting it wrong are proportionally larger, because the dependencies are everywhere.

Enterprise RevOps transformations fail most often because they underestimate the political dimension. Systems at enterprise scale are not just technical infrastructure — they encode power. Who owns the data, who can see what, which team's process becomes the default — these are not neutral questions. They affect headcount, budget, and influence. The change management plan must account for this reality explicitly, not pretend it does not exist.

The failure mode here is the big-bang transformation. A large-scale programme is announced, a new system is built in parallel, and a cutover date is set. Eighteen months later, the cutover is delayed. Twenty-four months later, the old system is still running alongside the new one. The transformation has become a permanent project rather than a completed change.

What works at this stage is phased delivery with measurable outcomes at each phase. Rather than a single transformation, design a sequence of smaller changes, each of which delivers a defined benefit and creates the foundation for the next. This approach generates proof points that build internal confidence, gives teams time to adapt, and allows the design to evolve based on what is actually learned in production rather than what was assumed in planning.

Governance structures matter at enterprise scale in a way they simply do not at startup scale. Clear ownership, documented decision rights, and defined escalation paths are not bureaucracy for its own sake — they are the mechanism by which large organisations make decisions without requiring the CEO to weigh in on every CRM field.

The Principles That Hold at Every Stage

Despite the differences, three principles apply regardless of organisational size.

Change must solve a visible problem. Operational changes that are justified by abstract principles — best practice, industry standard, what mature companies do — are almost never adopted at the rate of changes that solve a problem the team feels every day. Before designing any change, be able to articulate the specific pain it removes for the people who will live with it.

Adoption is a design problem, not a training problem. If a process requires extensive training to follow correctly, the process is too complex. The best-designed systems are followed intuitively because they make the right action the easiest action. Training is a supplement; it is not a substitute for good design.

The speed of change is constrained by the organisation's ability to absorb it. There is no universal right pace for transformation. The correct pace is the fastest rate at which genuine adoption — not compliance — can be achieved. Pushing faster than that rate does not accelerate transformation; it produces the appearance of change while the underlying behaviour stays the same.

RevOps transformations that land well are not the ones with the best technical design. They are the ones where the change approach was as carefully designed as the operational framework itself. The system is only as good as the adoption it achieves.
